title.narrative: OP 2.1: CBOs from south and west Mosul are selected and capacitated on mediation, negotiation, advocacy and on the early warning mechanisms; and providing early warning signals to prevent violent extremism.

description.narrative: A significant step was achieved by developing a transparent evaluation mechanism, complete with specific criteria, to select the Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) participating in the project from a pool of 18 organisations that participated in the previous project. In total, six CBOs were chosen based on their primary focus on supporting youth and women, thereby representing the targeted areas of the project. The evaluation process drew upon reports from the M&E Department, evaluations by recipients of the previous project, and feedback from beneficiaries of its activities. This comprehensive approach ensured a thorough assessment of each CBO's suitability for participation in the current project.The selected CBOs participated in a comprehensive orientation session conducted by TAD about the new project and signed collaboration agreements with the six chosen organisations. Following this, TAD launched a series of capacity-building workshops on mediation, negotiation, and advocacy. Participants then shared the knowledge gained with their respective staff to ensure widespread understanding and implementation.TAD has provided institutional capacity development packages for the six CBOs through coaching and mentoring the CBOs’ staff in media, finance, HR, and procurement departments, leading to improved documentation and communication of their activities, enhanced financial transparency and procurement processes, and increased visibility and engagement within the community.

title.narrative: Number of CBOs’ staff attended training courses on mediation, negotiation, advocacy and warning mechanisms (desegregated by subject and female/ male).

description.narrative: TAD invited 18 participants, with three from each CBO (nine men and nine women), to be trained in mediation, negotiation, advocacy, and early warning mechanisms. An experienced external trainer was hired to develop a training manual and conduct a three-day workshop. The trainer not only enhanced participants' knowledge but also assisted them in passing on the training to their colleagues. In August 2024, TAD began the capacity development for the six CBOs. TAD has developed their capacity institutionally by providing coaching and mentoring in media, finance, HR, and procurement. The media training, attended by six participants (one from each CBO, one woman and five men), provided their media and communication focal points/teams with essential skills in media coverage, photography, videography, news writing, and content creation. This training enabled them to document activities more effectively, create engaging content, and raise awareness about the issues they advocate for. Media officers were nominated to ensure the consistent application of these skills. The finance management, HR, and procurement training, attended by 13 participants (seven women and six men), focused on budgeting, expenditure tracking, and procurement processes, providing detailed guidance on contract terms and financial documentation. Delivered by the Finance Department staff, it ensured practical expertise. As a result, the CBOs have improved documentation and communication of their activities, enhanced financial transparency and procurement processes, and increased visibility and engagement within the community.

title.narrative: Number of CBOs identified and selected

description.narrative: TAD successfully completed selection of Partnered Community-Based Organizations (CBOs) in the current project. Recognising the significance of choosing organizations that had shown tangible and positive impact during the previous project, TAD implemented a transparent and independent selection mechanism. This entailed engaging the expertise of the Monitoring and Evaluation Department to devise a comprehensive performance evaluation system. The system collated data from various departments, including programme, financial, procurement, and communication, which were then scrutinised to inform the final selection. The evaluation process was carried out electronically, utilising a clear and standardised grading system to uphold objectivity. Upon completing the evaluation process, TAD extended invitations to the directors of the selected organisations to participate in the current project, with responses overwhelmingly positive, reflecting the organisations' enthusiasm and commitment. Subsequently, TAD convened a project kick-off meeting at their office in Mosul, where directors and members of the organisations were briefed on the project's objectives, duration, donors, contracting method, and terms. Detailed discussions were also held on project activities, action plans, financial and programmatic specifications, and anticipated media documentation methods. Currently, TAD is in the process of finalising contracts to be shared with the selected organisations for their review and signing purposes. These proactive measures by TAD underscore their dedication to ensuring the seamless implementation of the project and the sustained commitment of Partnered CBOs. In the beginning of May, after completing the contracting stage and finalising the budget for the projects and activities of the selected CBOs, TAD met with the six CBOs to sign the collaboration agreements that had previously been shared with them via email.

title.narrative: OP1.1: CSO partners have better planning and management capacity to advocate more effectively for women and girls’ rights in their communities.

description.narrative: Enhanced planning and management capacity of partners is a pivotal step towards more impactful advocacy for the rights of women and girls in their communities. By providing partners with strengthened capacity, NPA anticipates more informed and organized activities that address the specific needs and challenges faced by women and girls. Thus, contributing to positive and sustainable changes within the communities we are supporting.

title.narrative: Number of CSO partners’ staff attended Business Management ToT (disaggregated by female/male)

description.narrative: During August 2024, a five-day ToT was provided to the four partners on Business Management and Development. The business management modules covered key areas as follows: Entrepreneurship Foundation, leadership, Marketing Mix, Digital Marketing, marketing strategies, Business plan, Differentiation between small business and micro business, Safeguarding PSEA (Reporting Pathway), Financial Management, Project life cycle, Developing Business Plan, strategic planning. The trainer also reviewed the tools used by NPA partners and developed them accordingly. In addition, a three-day ToT was provided for three partners on Employment and Soft skills. The soft skills modules emphasized communication, teamwork, conflict resolution, Decision making, Negotiation Management, Time Management, Body language and emotional intelligence, which are crucial for building strong interpersonal relationships and creating a positive work environment. The purpose for these training sessions was to build the skill of livelihood officers and other staff of partners to provide similar training sessions to women and girls in targeted communities as part of the economic empowerment for these women and girls.

title.narrative: Number of trainings/ coaching/ mentoring sessions (desegregated by subject and female/male) provided for CSO partners.

description.narrative: During March 2024, a workshop on Visibility Guidelines provided by NPA Communication and Advocacy Consultant to three protection partners. This contributed to coordinating Presence and Visibility Strategies with NPA’s Partners, and other actors. Two other workshops were organised on Time Management and Organising Priorities to Avoid Stress. The workshops were inspired by Leadership Training ToT by Harvard University and Concern Worldwide that the WPE Project Manager participated in. The partners requested to have more refresher training and/or coaching on these topics, thus in December a refresher coaching session was provided to partners on reporting, lessons learnt and success stories writing. During February 2025, a two-day training on Conflict analysis, Conflict Sensitivity and Conflict Transformation was provided for the four partners in Duhok. The training was provided by the programme manager. During May 2025 a training in was held for partners on Humanitarian Photography, Videography, social media, and Storytelling for Humanitarian Work. The training was facilitated by the Communication and Advocacy Consultant, to strengthen the capacity of partners to ethically and effectively use advocacy communication tools including photography, video, and social media, keeping in mind do no harm and survivors centered approaches.

title.narrative: OP 3.2: Quality MHPSS support provided for women and girls 15+ who are survivors or at risk of Violence based on inequality between women and men in Dohuk Mosul.

description.narrative: In order to guarantee that survivors and those who are at risk receive knowledgeable and caring care, the MHPSS activities are created to include a wide range of mental health and psychosocial support. The objective is to build emotional well-being and resilience among the targeted demographic by addressing the unique difficulties and traumas related to violence based on inequality between women and men.

title.narrative: Number of women and girls 15+ received MHPSS services.

description.narrative: During the first quarter of the first year, the three protection partners were able to finalize the hiring process of psychologists. The psychologists initiated their work during March and started providing MHPSS services. While there are varied MHPSS services ranging from individual counselling and outdoor wellbeing group activities. The psychologists will facilitate some psychosocial activities when the need arises. For each case received, the psychologists formulate a treatment programme based on the cases’ needs and through observation of the social workers and other team members. Goals and a treatment plan are then identified to achieve personal, social and vocational development of the cases. The treatment plans are tailored to each case, however in general they focus to identify the signs and symptoms of any psychological disorder such as: depressive disorder, conversion disorder, shockwave disorder, etc. as well as medical history and what triggered these disorders, then based on these the psychologist initiates the treatment plan. One of the most common challenges is the lack of awareness of communities about the MHPSS, as any discussion about the psychological matters is considered stigmatizing and the survivors sometimes are scared about their families finding out they are meeting a psychologist, or the survivors don’t want to be referred out of the fear of the community. With that being said, the Yazidi displaced communities are slightly more open to receive the MHPSS counselling compared to the Muslim community in Mosul city. All three protection partners have delivered MHPSS services to a total of 1139 women and girls, since the start date of the programme in October 2023.

title.narrative: OP 3.3: Strengthened well-being of women and girls 15+ through community based psychosocial support, grass root advocacy, life skills, and recreational activities:

description.narrative: NPA and partners adopt a holistic approach to enhancing the well-being of women and girls. It involves a multifaceted strategy that incorporates community-based psychosocial support, grassroots advocacy, vocational training, and recreational activities. The aim is to create a supportive community environment that addresses the psychological, social, and recreational needs of women and girls. Through community-based psychosocial support, women and girls will have access to resources and services that promote mental and emotional health. Grassroots advocacy efforts aim to challenge societal norms and stereotypes, contributing to a more inclusive and supportive community.

title.narrative: Number of advocacy initiatives carried out by women and girls 15+ from the supported communities.

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the programme, 15 grass-root advocacy initiatives were carried out by women and girls in targeted communities. The initiatives that were carried out were: Supporting Women and Girls in Orphanages and Elderly Homes in Mosul city; This campaign aimed to improve living conditions by organizing activities like tree planting and garden clean-ups, providing much-needed emotional support. Integrating Women and Girls with Disabilities in Mosul city: This initiative raised awareness about the rights of women and girls with disabilities, working to protect them from sexual exploitation. Another one in Mosul was a campaign in Mosul to raise awareness about the safety and respect of female drivers. A campaign in coordination with the Directorate of Traffic in Mosul to survey the streets and install street bumps in areas where there is a frequent pedestrian movement or gets many traffic accidents. During the survey the community members were able to convey their messages and worries to the directorate and they received promised from the directorate that a pedestrian bridge will be built, cameras and traffic signs will be installed in their areas to ensure the safety of community members. A campaign was about raising awareness and early detection of Breast Cancer, in coordination with the Directorate of Health in Ninewa. The last one campaign during the reporting period was about the importance of education for girls and the role of parents in encouraging continuity of girls’ education, the campigncampaign targeted 25 girls with their parents to discuss the challenges of girls’ education as well as the importance of education for the girls to have a brighter future. Two other initiatives were carried out in Shariya town, one was building the advocacy skills of women and girls; one of the PSS beneficiaries developed some materials to train women and girls from her community on advocacy skills within their families to advocate for their rights and needs. The second one was planting trees; launched in July 2024, was led by six girls who, after participating in the advocacy sessions, came up with the idea of planting trees in specific areas of Sharya non-camp. They approached the municipality, conveyed the importance of planting trees for the community and how they protect the environment, and successfully obtained approval for the initiative. The municipality was supportive throughout the planning phase. Due to weather conditions, the group had to wait for a suitable time, and by the end of September, they began the tree-planting process with the support of an engineer from the Sharya municipality. Another one was about cleaning the camp of Bersive 1; 17 girls after finishing the course of the PSS on advocacy, approached the camp management with their plan to clean the camps from waste and to promote a healthier environment. Impressed by their efforts, the camp management called for any other NGO along with them to support the girls. Finally, a day was specified, the girls, the camp management and two other NGOs started cleaning camp campaign. During the reporting period from October 2025 to December 2025 , 30 women and girls divided into in two groups in BWOCD centare in Musol, jointly planned women-led advocacy initiatives under the grassroots advocacy programme to address the inequality between men and women inequality and violence against women and girls (VAWG). They prioritized issues including domestic violence, digital blackmail, early marriage, divorce/suicide risks, and community concerns like poor services, overcrowded schools, inadequate health care, unsafe streets, waste, and water shortages. BWOCD provided facilitation on planning, messaging, duty bearers, and coordination, preparing participants for implementation pending official approvals. Also, since the start of the programme in October 2023 through December 2025, a total of 475 men and boys have participated in positive masculinity sessions provided by our protection partners. Also, another initiative was conducted by BWOCD in October, the second initiative promoted early breast cancer detection by coordinating women’s access to clinical breast examinations and ultrasound. Nine women were screened, and seven were found to have breast-related concerns (e.g., lumps) requiring follow-up. The initiative leader and project team coordinated with charitable clinics in Mosul to provide the required examinations and ultrasounds free of charge. The initiative was proposed by women beneficiaries after an initial awareness-raising session delivered by a specialized female gynaecologist in coordination with the Directorate of Health, which covered early detection methods and clinical breast examinations. The first session revealed a significant knowledge gap, prompting a shift from awareness to practical screening support.After implementation, linkages with local health authorities improved, and women reported greater confidence in requesting and accessing services from the Directorate of Health, reflecting stronger trust and engagement.During the reporting period, BWOCD conducted an advocacy initiative session aimed at raising awareness of women’s rights and strengthening communication and leadership skills. The initiative addressed topics such as violence, harassment, and social challenges. As a result, participants gained knowledge, built confidence to express their needs, and developed stronger networks, leading to greater self-advocacy and active engagement in their communities 13 women have participated in the session.

title.narrative: Percentage of outreached women and girls 15+ attending psychosocial and reintegration activities

description.narrative: The psychosocial and reintegration activities within the programme are crucial components that underpin the effectiveness and impact of the advocacy efforts at grass-roots level. With structured sessions focusing on communication skills, equality between men and women, leadership, advocacy message development, and accountability, women and girls are equipped with the knowledge and skills necessary for effective advocacy initiatives at family and community level. These activities not only empower women and girls to communicate their experiences and advocate for their rights but also foster a sense of solidarity, empathy and collective action.

OP 3.6: Increased advocacy and awareness for implementing Law No.8 of 2021 (Yazidi Female Survivors Law).

description.narrative: NPA and partners had meetings with stakeholders to understand the most pressing needs of the ISIS survivors. NPA and BWOCD have hold a meeting with IOM to discuss the priorities of the survivors and what added value can NPA and partners do. The meeting once again gave NPA and partners the assurance that more awareness to survivors and their families is needed especially in Sinjar district, as well as connecting survivors with governmental stakeholders to ensure their voices are heard.

title.narrative: Number of workshops and FGD/meetings for survivor regarding the Law No.8 of 2021

description.narrative: During May and June 2024, two workshops were held by PDO for ISIS survivors. During the workshops the survivors discussed what has been done and what can be done to improve the lives of the survivors and implement the Iraqi Law No.8 of 2021 - Yazidi Female Survivors Law All survivors agreed that more awareness is necessary about the implementation of the law and the content of the law, so that the survivors have sufficient knowledge on how to claim their rights and compensation. The survivors agreed that PDO’s approach of engaging survivors with these workshops and empowering them to demand their rights, is the correct methodology to ensure the sustainability of efforts and achievements of better impacts. An eight-day training course was conducted by BWOCD for ISIS survivors in Sinjar. The main goal was to enhance participants' skills to support their recovery and future advocacy efforts. The course included eight structured training sessions: The first two days focused on the Yazidi Women Survivors Law, where participants learned about its key provisions, how to register under the law, and its importance in securing survivors’ rights. The next two days covered advocacy training, teaching participants techniques and strategies to promote the Yazidi Women Survivors Law and defend survivors’ rights. A one-day life skills training session emphasized resilience, emotional well-being, and personal development, helping participants in their holistic recovery. The public speaking training on another day-built participants' confidence to deliver impactful awareness sessions about the challenges Yazidi survivors face. Communication skills were developed during a dedicated day of training, focusing on conveying messages clearly and building rapport during advocacy efforts. Participants also learned about networking and relationship building to strengthen their advocacy work with community leaders and organizations. Finally, a day was dedicated to negotiation skills, equipping participants to navigate sensitive situations effectively.

title.narrative: Number of meetings conducted with relevant stakeholders including the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, the Ministry of Migration and Displacement, the Women Committee of the Iraqi Parliament and others to discuss the implementation of the Law No.8 of 2021

description.narrative: During the first year of the programme, as part of the coordination and/or raising awareness about the struggles of survivors and best methodologies to support them, eight meetings were conducted with stakeholders. These meetings were with the NRC, IRC Warjen organization, Survivors Network and Survivors directorate and Progress in Peace and Hope Maker Organization to reach survivors, and with IOM to obtain and distribute publications and informational materials related to the Yazidi Survivors Law. This partnership ensured that survivors had access to accurate and up-to-date guidance on their rights and the legal processes available to them. During April 2025, four meetings were held in Baghdad by NPA’s partner PDO, with Deputy Minister of Labor and Social Affairs, Director-General of the Planning and Development Department, Advisor to the Prime Minister, Dr. Khalaf Sinjari, and Coordinator of the Criminal Justice Committee, Mr. Hassan Jamil Khalid, Special Meeting with the Minister of Migration and Displaced Persons. A formal letter of recommendations was shared with these high officials that contained suggestions related to support for survivors in terms of education, MHPPS, compensations as well as simplifying procedures so that all survivors have knowledge and access to their entitled compensations.

OP 1.5: CSO partners are strengthened to become active actors in facilitating, mobilizing, and empowering their communities to become more stable.

description.narrative: The CSOs, CSOs, RSCs and ONSA have developed a shared understanding of the use of the PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System in the Ninewa context. The discussions supported better coordination between national and local actors, clarified roles and approaches, and informed the development of practical tools and action plans to guide community-based PVE activities and monitoring throughout the project

title.narrative: Number of CSO partners’ staff attended training courses on PVE toolkit, enhancing their understanding of the drivers of violent extremism and equipping them with tools and strategies to prevent and counteract its spread within their communities.

description.narrative: Four coordination and technical sessions were conducted to strengthen the adaptation and filling of the PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System (EWS) Guide. The process began with an internal technical meeting with TAD, which focused on reviewing the PVE Toolkit and EWS Guide and agreeing on key priorities for contextual adaptation. This was followed by a joint session bringing together TAD, CBOs, and RSCs to contextualise the PVE tools and align them with the community-level early warning indicators identified through consultations. Building on this work, a technical coordination session was held with ONSA to ensure that community-based EWS approaches were aligned with national PVE frameworks and policy directions. The process concluded with a planning and coordination session involving NPA and the four CSOs, during which action plans were finalised, PVE materials were developed, and EWS indicators were integrated into project implementation and monitoring tools, ensuring coherence and consistency across all partners.

OP 2.3: CBOs and CSOs, community representatives, local authorities and other stakeholders contribute to developing effective and contextually localized plans of intervention and implementing interventions conducive to prevention of violent extremism and stabilisation.

description.narrative: The TAD programme and MEAL team have created an online form and advertised a call for interest post on their social media account for community members who are willing to participate in the RSCs voluntary opportunity in the six areas of the project.TAD received a total of 508 applications (393 male and 115 female) from individuals who have filled in their information to be part of the RSCs in their areas. After the application period ended, TAD formed a selection committee to analyse the data they received and select the RSC members.TAD selected 24 community members (15 male and nine female), with four representatives from each of the six targeted areas, and signed a code of conduct to establish an official committee. These selected individuals were then introduced to the community and local authorities. Additionally, TAD hired an external international expert to empower RSCs through capacity building trainings on preventing violent extremism (PVE) and to develop, design, and implement effective community initiatives.CBOs programme staff have improved their PVE awareness, designing community initiatives and the analysis of the threats in the areas that operating in that aiming to reduce the level of violence and responding to the PVE indicators that were determined in the community consultation conducted by the CBOs and the RSCs in the targeted areas.Community-led initiatives in six areas of Ninewa strengthened resilience by addressing vulnerabilities to violent extremism, fostering cooperation between communities and local authorities, and promoting peaceful coexistence through inclusive dialogue, empowerment of local actors, and locally driven solutions for reintegration and tolerance. The technical and operational capabilities of TAD and the six CBO were enhanced through the review and adaptation of the PVE toolkit and EWS guide. A report template on Early Warning Mechanism indicators was developed to support community awareness campaigns, foster partnerships with stakeholders, and aid in creating PVE-responsive monitoring and evaluation tools. These efforts aim to enable NPA and its partners to deliver comprehensive PVE reintegration and engagement, promoting resilience and preventing violent extremism within Ninewa communities.Building on previous efforts, community-led initiatives in the six project areas of Ninewa strengthened resilience by addressing VE indicators identified and prioritised by communities during consultations and dialogue sessions. Key interventions—including the “Echo of Peace” digital platform, community policing training, permanent community–police forums, and complaints mechanisms—enabled meaningful participation of youth and women, improved public services, resolved local electricity and road safety issues, and created structured platforms for raising community concerns. These activities reinforced trust in local authorities, strengthened accountability, and contributed to early prevention of violence while promoting peaceful coexistence and inclusive governance.

title.narrative: Number of community members capacitated and empowered through trainings to establish Resilient and Stabilisation Committees (RSCs), the selected community members will be inclusive and representative i.e., including women.

description.narrative: A committee consisting of the MEAL Officer, Project Manager, and Project Coordinators from TAD was formed to develop a mechanism for including target groups in a way that positively reflects the project and future interventions. This mechanism involved creating selection criteria for community members to be capacitated and engaged with the programme to implement community initiatives. The criteria were inclusive and representative, with special consideration given to vulnerable social groups such as women, youth, minorities, IDPs, and Persons with Disabilities (PwD). The TAD Programme and MEAL team created an online form and advertised a call for interest on their social media account for community members willing to volunteer for RSCs in the six areas of the project. The form included detailed questions covering various aspects such as educational level, participation in civil society, and knowledge related to preventing violent extremism, allowing for the fair and transparent selection of community members. The application forms were announced and disseminated via social media, distributed to partner organisations for further dissemination within their communities, and shared within various working groups and with heads of administrative units in those areas. This ensured that community members who met the criteria could apply to engage with the programme and implement effective community initiatives. TAD received a total of 508 applications (393 men and 115 women) from individuals interested in joining the RSCs in their areas. Following the application period, TAD formed a selection committee to analyse the data received and select the RSC members. To provide the selected RSCs with the tools to prevent violent extremism and promote stability, a training was conducted to the RSCs members. This training utilised a practical, hands-on approach, focusing on applying key frameworks. Participants learnt to analyse their initiatives through a SWOT analysis, establish clear and achievable goals using SMART criteria, and manage the initiatives effectively through a comprehensive lifecycle approach. Additionally, the training equipped the RSCs with problem-solving skills through the problem tree exercise and stakeholder analysis, enabling them to navigate their relationships and develop strategies for collaboration and resistance management. This training empowers community leaders and RSCs to design and implement impactful initiatives, ultimately fostering a more stable and peaceful environment.

title.narrative: Number of community initiatives implemented by Local RSC members and CBOs (five community initiatives per targeted area) each initiative reaching 500-1,000 beneficiaries.

description.narrative: Between April and June 2025, a total of twelve community-led initiatives were implemented by TAD in coordination and facilitation of the CBOs and involvement of the RSC members across six areas of Ninewa: South of Mosul (Al-Shora sub-district, Al-Qayyara sub-district, and Hammam Al-Alil sub-district) and West of Mosul (Al-Ayadiyah sub-district, Qayrawan sub-district, and Sinjar district). These initiatives were carried out to enhanced resilience of local communities through inclusive, community-led initiatives that reduce vulnerabilities to violent extremism and foster trust between citizens and authorities. Collectively, the initiatives directly engaged 931 community members (approximately 320 women and 611 men) while reaching several thousand additional individuals through media products, public events, and awareness campaigns. The activities reflect significant progress towards strengthening local resilience, promoting peaceful coexistence, and addressing drivers of violent extremism through context-specific and inclusive approaches. Six initiatives were implemented during April. In Hammam Al-Alil, the “Voice of Moderation” initiative engaged 20 participants (eight women, 12 men), including religious leaders, community police, and community influencers, in workshops on moderate speech. The follow-up awareness campaign reached over 500 residents through public engagement in markets and neighbourhoods. In Qayrawan, “Bridges of Peace” mobilised 57 women from diverse backgrounds, including educators, youth, activists, and religious leaders, to discuss their roles in preventing violent extremism, producing media outputs that emphasised coexistence. In Sinjar, “Sinjar Victory for Peace” strengthened the capacity of 22 journalists (11 women, 11 men) to distinguish between freedom of expression, hate speech, and positive speech that supports peace and prevents violence and extremism. In Al-Shora, “Learning Together” reached 20 children (11 girls, nine boys) from returnee and host families by providing school supplies, psychosocial support, and recreational activities. The initiative-built trust among families and reinforced the right to education for vulnerable children. In Al-Ayadiyah, “Peace Made by Education, led by the Teacher” gathered 20 teachers and local officials in a workshop and dialogue session to highlight education’s role in preventing violent extremism. Teachers were trained to identify early signs of radicalisation, encouraged to openly discuss sensitive issues, and recognised as the “first line of defence” in shaping a tolerant generation. Finally, in Al-Qayyara, “A_Safe_Environment” linked community stability to environmental action by installing 60 waste containers carrying peace messages, supported by a digital campaign that actively engaged youth, particularly young women. Six initiatives were implemented during June. In Hammam Al-Alil, the “No Drugs Among Us” campaign engaged 58 participants (eight women, 50 men) in a conference coinciding with the International Day Against Drug Abuse. It combined educational sessions, theatre, and brochure distribution, reinforcing cooperation between citizens and authorities and leading to follow-up action by community police. In Al-Ayadiyah, the “Mobility Disability Support” initiative improved access to public services for persons with disabilities by installing ramps at three government offices. The intervention had immediate impact, with beneficiaries—including an elderly woman in a wheelchair—reporting restored dignity and independent access. In Al-Shora, the “Bridges” initiative engaged 20 participants (seven women, 13 men) in capacity-building workshops that concluded with the creation of the Al-Shora Volunteer Team. This group now serves as a nucleus for sustained community action and was formally recognised by the sub-district director. In Qayrawan (Tal Qasab), the “Music and Art Unite Us” festival gathered 83 participants (23 women, 60 men) from Arab, Kurdish, and Yazidi communities in a shared cultural space for the first time in years. The event marked unprecedented female participation and received wide media coverage. In Sinjar, “A Better Life for Persons with Disabilities” convened 150 participants (60 women, 90 men) for a public film screening on disability rights. The initiative shifted community perceptions and inspired individuals with disabilities to engage in activism. Finally, in Al-Qayyara, the “Protecting MasterCard from Hacking and Digital Blackmail” campaign distributed 500 brochures, and hosted awareness stands to address rising digital fraud cases. The initiative simplified technical concepts for vulnerable groups, particularly the elderly, and gained credibility through close collaboration with local authorities and community police. During September 2025, five community-led initiatives were implemented across Hammam Al-Alil, Tal Afar, Al-Shura, Qayrawan, and Al-Qayyarah under the “Enhancing Stability in Conflict-Affected Communities in Iraq” programme. Collectively, the initiatives reached 174 direct beneficiaries (62 female and 112 male), and promoted innovative mechanisms for dialogue, community safety, accountability, and youth engagement. The activities contributed to strengthening local stability, enhancing collaboration between communities and authorities, and promoting inclusive civic participation across conflict-affected areas. In Hammam Al-Alil, Al-Erada Organisation for Relief & Development convened a dialogue session introducing the digital platform “Echo of Peace,” designed to foster social cohesion and rebuild trust in the post-ISIS recovery period. The session gathered 27 participants (9 female and 18 male), among them the District Director, tribal sheikhs, Mukhtars, and the Community Police Director. Discussions focused on digital mechanisms for community engagement, empowering women and youth participation, and establishing an official virtual space for community initiatives. The strong institutional presence reinforced local ownership of the platform, which youth participants described as a sustainable tool for promoting peace-oriented initiatives. In Tal Afar, the Nama Organisation for Human Development conducted a two-day training on community policing, organisational skills, problem-solving, and conflict resolution at the Community Police Headquarters. The activity involved 40 participants, including (16 female and 24 male). The training strengthened understanding of community policing principles and prepared participants to establish local community forums to enhance cooperation with authorities. Participants demonstrated strong teamwork, expressed readiness to form volunteer support groups, and highlighted the impact of weak services and economic hardship on youth vulnerability. In Al-Shura, the Peer Organisation for Youth Development launched the official Al-Shura Community Police Forum, a permanent dialogue platform aimed at promoting safety and preventing violent extremism in the district. description.narrative: In November 2024, a three-day workshop titled “PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System Guide for NPA CSOs and CBOs" was held in Erbil. TAD organised the workshop, and the NPA PVE consultant facilitated it. This workshop brought together representatives from TAD, CBOs, and sub-national countering violence and extremism in Ninewa to learn about tools and strategies for Preventing Violent Extremism (PVE). The training focused on using the PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System Guide to help CBOs address risks and respond to threats. Participants engaged in discussions, practical exercises, and shared experiences to develop effective ways to prevent violence and strengthen their work in their communities. Additionally, a report template on Early Warning Mechanism indicators was developed to support community awareness campaigns, foster partnerships with stakeholders, and aid in the creation of PVE-responsive monitoring and evaluation tools. The workshop empowered the attendees' skills to evaluate risks and enhance community resilience, aiming to reduce violence and address PVE indicators identified during community consultations conducted after the workshop. The active involvement of community members fostered trust and ownership, leading to sustainable and impactful interventions. A total of 20 participants attended this training (12 men and 8 women). TAD conducted a three-day training for the National Committee for Countering Violent Extremism (NCCVE) in Erbil from 13 to 15 September 2025, aimed at strengthening Iraq’s national capacity on the Preventing Violent Extremism Toolkit and Early Warning System Guide (PVE Toolkit and EWSG) developed by NPA. The workshop brought together 29 participants, including the Head of NCCVE, heads of the Early Warning Sub-Committees from multiple Iraqi governorates, representatives from the National Security Advisory, the Iraqi National Security Service, and the Iraqi National Intelligence Service, as well as academics, civil society actors, and media representatives, reflecting a broad, multi-sectoral approach to prevention. The training focused on enhancing participants’ understanding of the Early Warning System and its key indicators, alongside practical guidance on the application of PVE toolkits for monitoring, analysing, and responding to emerging risks. Participants were trained to use these toolkits to design preventive initiatives, develop monitoring indicators, and formulate early response strategies, while integrating conflict-sensitive approaches and gender considerations to ensure inclusive interventions. The workshop also emphasised how information collected by local monitoring teams can be systematically used to inform policy decisions and coordinate timely action across federal and local authorities. The active engagement of NCCVE, including its leadership and sub-committee heads, demonstrated the Government of Iraq’s commitment to institutionalising the EWS within state structures. The training successfully unified methodologies across governorates, enhanced coordination between central and local authorities, and strengthened participants’ capacity to identify early signs of violent extremism and respond effectively. Participants confirmed that the workshop provided them with practical analytical tools, improved their confidence in applying the PVE toolkits, and reinforced a proactive, evidence-based approach to preventing violent extremism across Iraq.

In Al-Qayyara, Creativity Foundation for Human Rights amplified youth and community perspectives, particularly regarding civic participation and digital risks, engaging 20 participants (six women and 14 men). A total of 124 participants (73 men, 51 women) took part.During the reporting period (January – March 2026), NPA, in partnership with TAD and six local CBOs, facilitated six result-based dialogue and community consultation sessions across conflict-affected areas in Ninewa Governorate, including Hammam Al-Alil, Al-Qayyara, Al-Ayadhiyya, Al-Shura, Sinjar, and Qayrawan. The sessions brought together 144 participants (106 male and 38 female), including representatives from local authorities, service directorates, civil society organizations, community leaders, youth representatives, women, and other community stakeholders. The activities aimed to strengthen community engagement, improve coordination between communities and local institutions, and support locally driven approaches to stabilization, service delivery, and prevention efforts. In Qayrawan, Youth Bridge Development Organization facilitated a dialogue session attended by 41 participants (40 male and one female), bringing together representatives from the local administration, service directorates, civil society actors, and community leaders to discuss post-conflict recovery challenges affecting stability and service delivery. Discussions focused on infrastructure rehabilitation, water shortages, municipal services, environmental concerns, and the need to strengthen coordination between local authorities and communities to support sustainable recovery and social cohesion. In Sinjar, Tomooh Organization for Development conducted a dialogue session with 20 participants (12 male and eight female), focusing on environmental and municipal service challenges affecting public health and living conditions. Participants discussed deteriorating roads, waste management, limited green spaces, and infrastructure gaps, while proposing practical community-based initiatives and stronger coordination between the municipality, local authorities, and communities to improve service delivery and environmental conditions. In Al-Ayadhiyya, Nama Organization facilitated a result-based dialogue session attended by 20 participants (17 male and three female), focusing on challenges related to water access, agriculture, health services, and municipal service delivery. Participants discussed overcrowded classrooms, shortages in school infrastructure, double and triple-shift systems, instability among teaching staff, and school dropout risks linked to economic hardship. Discussions addressed water shortages, school dropout, drug use, online blackmail, and the protection of green spaces. Participants emphasized the importance of awareness initiatives, youth engagement activities, and stronger cooperation between schools, community police, religious institutions, and local authorities to strengthen social cohesion and reduce risks associated with violent extremism and social exclusion. Across all six sessions, participants jointly identified practical and context-sensitive recommendations aimed at improving service delivery, strengthening institutional coordination, enhancing community participation, supporting women and youth engagement, and reinforcing social cohesion and local stability. title.narrative: Number of reports developed by NPA CSO on any rise or fall with respect to the Early Warning Mechanism indicators.

description.narrative: Following a comprehensive training facilitated by the NPA PVE Consultant on Preventing Violent Extremism Toolkit and Early Warning System Guide, and the identification of violent extremism indicators, staff from the six CBOs and members of the Resilience and Stabilisation Committees (RSCs) were equipped with the skills needed to detect threats that could undermine community stability in Ninewa. Participants were provided with a standardised reporting template to guide their assessments, enabling consistent and structured analysis across different communities. Using this tool, the CBOs conducted localised assessments and submitted detailed reports highlighting key indicators of violent extremism. A total of 12 reports were produced by the CBOs and RSCs, and further developed by the NPA PVE Consultant. These reports were then reviewed and analysed collaboratively by NPA and TAD to assess trends in the rise or fall of risk levels in relation to the Early Warning Mechanism. The reports drew on a combination of input from stabilisation committees, feedback from community members, and the CBOs' contextual understanding of their operating environments. The goal of this process was the identification of a refined set of violent extremism indicators that now serve as a strategic framework to guide future community-based interventions. These indicators will inform the design and implementation of targeted initiatives that aim to mitigate risks early and strengthen local resilience against radicalisation. The indicators will be monitored and then rise and fall reports will be developed on accordingly.

The primary goal was to involve local communities in identifying and prioritizing indicators of violent extremism. This participatory approach ensured that the Early Warning Mechanism tool was informed by local insights and experiences, enhancing its relevance and effectiveness.Building on this foundation, CBOs applied their training from the PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System as they began the consultation sessions. These indicators served as a reference framework to guide the evaluation of community risk levels and the shaping of relevant interventions. title.narrative: Number of community consultation sessions conducted by CBOs with local community representatives.

description.narrative: TAD supervised partnered CBOs to conduct six community consultations and sensitisation sessions in the six locations of the project in Ninewa. Each session aimed to engage local communities and stakeholders in identifying and prioritising community needs and challenges related to basic infrastructure and essential services. A total of 120 participants attended these sessions. In Al-Shoura District, Mosul, on 15 July 2024, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) gathered to discuss key issues. They identified a lack of staff in schools, leading to overcrowded classrooms, low educational standards, and high dropout rates. Additionally, many children lacked identification documents, hindering their education and causing feelings of exclusion. The Al-Shoura Health Centre faced a shortage of medical equipment and specialist doctors, and farmers in the district struggled with insufficient government support, resulting in low living standards and high unemployment. Proposed solutions included recruiting and retaining more teachers, facilitating the issuance of identification documents, increasing medical equipment and specialist doctors, and developing training programmes for farmers. On 11 July 2024, in Hammam Al-Alil District, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) addressed issues such as excessive livestock and stray dogs in residential areas, neglect of public funds, lack of job opportunities, and the need for support for vulnerable families. Proposed solutions involved conducting awareness sessions for livestock owners, raising awareness through campaigns, setting up a market for local artisans and craftsmen to showcase and sell their products, and providing school supplies to children from vulnerable families. In Sinjar District, on 24 July 2024, 20 participants (six women and 14 men) discussed judiciary instability due to political conflicts, lack of a dedicated building for Sinjar General Hospital, agricultural challenges, and education shortages. They proposed forming an administration to release financial allocations, allocating land and funds for a new hospital building, providing state support through affordable agricultural inputs, and rehabilitating damaged schools while building new ones. On 18 July 2024, in Al-Ayadhiyah District, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) identified issues such as the lack of a maternity room, scarcity of treatments for chronic diseases, lack of laboratory equipment, and unemployment of widows and divorcees. Proposed solutions included assigning staff to the maternity room at least two days a week, providing health cards for low-income individuals, acquiring essential laboratory equipment, and offering sewing machines or vocational training for widows and divorcees. In Qayrawan District, on 22 July 2024, 22 participants (seven women and 13 men) highlighted conflicts between farmers and the North Oil Company, lack of school buildings due to land ownership issues, loss of identification documents complicating school enrolment, and motorcycle-related traffic accidents. Proposed solutions were to let farmers use their land for growing crops and grazing animals, facilitate land transfer procedures for school construction, coordinate the issuance of identification documents for children, and ban unlicensed motorcycles while ensuring compliance with safety standards. Finally, in Qayyarah District, on 14 July 2024, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) discussed air pollution from a nearby sanitary landfill, problems with the Angolan Company seizing agricultural lands, obstacles in receiving benefits and rights for martyrs’ families, and water pollution from sewage in the Tigris River. Proposed solutions included relocating the landfill site, compensating affected farmers, simplifying procedures for martyrs’ families to receive benefits, and developing sewage infrastructure to prevent contamination of the river. Between July and September 2025, the six CBOs implemented a total of 12 result-based dialogue sessions across Al-Ayadiyah, Hammam Al-Alil, Sinjar, Qayrawan, Al-Qayyarah and Al-Shura. July focused on preparation and coordination, while all sessions were conducted during the implementation period. In total, the activity engaged 236 participants (98 female and 138 males) of the total participants of the sessions. Which each included 20 participants, except the session conducted by Youth Bridge Development Organisation in Qayrawan, which involved 31 participants to ensure balanced representation from RSC members, local authorities and community representatives, creating an inclusive platform to address outstanding service needs. Below are the details of the dialogues conducted: In Al-Ayadiyah, Nama Organisation for Human Development conducted two advocacy sessions engaging a total of 42 participants. The sessions addressed the need to establish a dedicated Community Police Unit, water scarcity, and the growing impact of desertification, as well as municipal service gaps such as debris accumulation, insufficient cleaning personnel, weak street lighting, unemployment, and lack of economic empowerment opportunities. The organisation concluded the activity by receiving letters of thanks from the District Administration and Police. In Hammam Al-Alil, Al-Erada Organization for Relief & Development conducted two dialogue sessions engaging 40 participants. The sessions generated commitments from the health, education, water and municipal departments, including improving heating and cooling in schools, repairing the high-thrust water pump for Juhayna Complex, installing lighting poles, allocating grants and soft loans for farmers, establishing a government seedling nursery, and installing transformers in low-voltage areas. The organisation received appreciation letters from the Community Police and District Administration. In Sinjar, Tomooh Organization for Development conducted two dialogue sessions with 40 participants. The sessions highlighted acute water shortages in Azadi and Weiran Shar, resulting in advocacy for allocating 637 million IQD for water network rehabilitation. Education sector challenges, including the need for new school buildings, classroom maintenance, and urgent staffing reinforcements, were also addressed. A key achievement was the successful resolution of the water crisis in both neighbourhoods. Tomooh received letters of thanks from the Water, Health, and Education Directorates. In Qairawan, Youth Bridge Development Organization conducted two dialogue sessions involving 59 participants. The sessions brought together service department representatives and community representatives to raise concerns about limited municipal equipment, budget shortages, and issues of fair representation. These efforts led to a formal commitment from a Nineveh Provincial Council member to follow up on the issues raised and resulted in the inclusion of Qairawan’s internal roads in the official Reconstruction Plan. Additionally, five complaints boxes were distributed to strengthen communication between communities and authorities. In Al-Qayyarah, Creativity Foundation for Human Rights conducted two dialogue sessions engaging 40 participants. The sessions focused on water and electricity challenges, resulting in the immediate resolution of a vulnerable family's water access problem and the rapid intervention of the electricity department to resolve an overloaded transformer complaint. The organisation received several letters of appreciation, including from the National Security Advisor’s Office, Mosul District Administration, the Police Directorate, and the Municipality. In Al-Shura, Peer Organization for Youth Development conducted two dialogue sessions attended by 35 participants. The sessions mapped priority issues related to water, electricity, roads, school materials, unemployment, and limited youth services. Peer also launched the Al-Shura Community Police Forum, composed of 15 members, which has become a sustainable platform for strengthening cooperation between communities and law enforcement, ensuring women’s voices are represented in addressing service gaps and contributing to local stability. Peer Organisation received letters of appreciation from the District Administration and Police. The 12 dialogue sessions produced tangible results across the six areas of intervention in Ninewa. In Al-Ayadiyah, gaps in municipal services and community policing were addressed, while Hammam Al-Alil saw improvements in school facilities, water infrastructure, and agricultural support. In Sinjar, water shortages and education challenges were successfully resolved, and in Qayrawan, community concerns influenced the official Reconstruction Plan and strengthened communication channels with authorities. Al-Qayyarah benefited from immediate solutions to water and electricity issues, and in Al-Shura, the establishment of the Community Police Forum created a sustainable platform for community–police cooperation and inclusive decision-making. Collectively, these outcomes enhanced trust in local authorities, empowered communities to voice their priorities freely, and contributed to greater resilience and stability across conflict-affected areas of Ninewa.

Apart from that, BWOCD had to halt their activities in one of the neighbourhoods due to tribal tensions that increased and caused security concerns. During the reporting period July–September 2025, BWOCD implemented a serios of awareness-raising activities, including distributing brochures, , and creating a success-story video, to increase community knowledge and participation. Following the NPA training on Communication with Communities, Do No Harm, and Safeguarding, BWOCD staff were able to engage communities more safely and effectively, building trust and credibility despite ongoing security challenges in some neighborhoods.To date, protection partners have reached a total of 7928 community members through awareness-raising sessions on women and girls’ well-being and empowerment.

In order to ensure sustainability and foster knowledge sharing, each partner will formulate a comprehensive plan outlining how they intend to share knowledge and effectively apply the obtained skills in their respective contexts. title.narrative: OP 3.4: Improved social support and recreational activities are provided for men and boys 15+.

description.narrative: The program recognizes the important role that men and boys play in fostering an inclusive and equitable society. By increasing their awareness, the programme aims to promote a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by women and the importance of achieving equality between men and women. Through tailored masculinity programme, the awareness of men and boys regarding equality will be increased and they will be encouraged to become advocates for women's rights and contribute to dismantling existing disparities. The curricula for the masculinity sessions have been developed, as changes are needed based on the lessons learnt of the prior programme.

title.narrative: Number of men and boys 15+ attended social support and recreational activities, desegregated by location

description.narrative: One of the lessons learnt from the previous programmes is that engaging with men and boys is different than engaging with women and girls. Men and boys have their own needs and requests, for example, during the mornings they are busy working or going to school, thus the partners consult with them before planning any activity. Men and boys also are less interested in awareness sessions thus any activity that is targeted towards them should have some recreational and entertainment aspects. As a result, NPA and partners have prioritized engaging men and boys in its activities to foster their role as positive partners in promoting equality and building inclusive communities. Through dedicated sessions, men and boys developed greater awareness of human rights, social justice, and the impact of emotions and behaviors on family and community dynamics. These safe and reflective spaces encouraged open dialogue, helping men and boys to challenge harmful stereotypes, adopt healthier attitudes, and embrace values of cooperation, empathy, and shared responsibility. Therefore, NPA partners were able to engage 414 men and boys in social support and recreational activities, and through their involvement, men and boys began reshaping their roles as active contributors to equality and non-violence, laying important foundations for stronger families and more cohesive and just communities in the long term this was evident in the success stories that were observed by partners and surveys that were carried out by NPA and partners’ MEAL after the end of each session, where men expressed openness to support their female family members and better understanding of equality between men and women. During the reporting period, all three protection partners delivered positive masculinity sessions for men and boys aged 15+ across Bajid Kandala camp, Chamishku camp, and the BWOCD Center in Mosul, creating safe spaces for open dialogue on equality between men and women and social norms, power dynamics, and different forms of violence, and their link to violence against women and girls (VAWG). In total, 70 male participants took part (21 through PDO in Bajid Kandala & Chamishku, 36 through Emma in two groups over three sessions, and 13 through BWOCD in Mosul over three consecutive days). Overall, the sessions improved participants’ understanding of biological sex and socially learned roles, encouraged shared household responsibilities, and promoted respectful, non-violent communication, notably, 7 of 21 PDO participants reported clear behavior changes at home, such as regularly supporting family members with domestic tasks and being more mindful during conflicts. Also, since the start of the programme in October 2023, a total of 555 men and boys have participated in positive masculinity sessions provided by our protection partners.

title.narrative: OP 4.1: Improved economic skills for conflict affected women through vocational trainings and business management skills development.

description.narrative: The programme aims to empower women by providing them with practical knowledge and expertise relevant to improbity skills, as well as small business operations. Business management skills development will focus on entrepreneurial skills such as financial literacy, market understanding, marketing of products and services and strategic planning. By improving economic skills through these targeted efforts, the project aims to enable women to establish and manage small businesses effectively, fostering economic independence and resilience for women and their families.

title.narrative: Number of soft and employable skills trainings conducted, desegregated by type of training

description.narrative: During March 2024, one training course for young men and women that extended for six days was provided by PDO in coordination with Hevi Volunteer group and DCVAW on how to build skills and enhance the capabilities of new graduates to enable them to obtain and reach the necessary resources that enable them to rely completely on themselves and develop their mental, psychological and physical capabilities. It is worth noting that the course covered more than one different topic by professional trainers, including journalists, some of them who work in the government, as well as lawyers and trainers in the field of self-development. During the last quarter of the first year, three soft and employable skills training sessions were provided for the newly graduates and other women looking to get into the workforce. The main topics discussed were Self-esteem, Emotional management, Creativity Decision making and problem solving, Effective communication, Negotiation, Teamwork, Time and stress management. As well as good practices for C.V. writing and interview skills. The training session took place in Duhok and Ninewa. In April 2025 BWOCD ran a Soft Skills workshop for 15 young female graduates from marginalized communities in Mosul. The training focused on CV writing, interview readiness, and protection from sexual exploitation, while also providing a safe space for participants to share experiences and build mutual support. During the reporting period, three soft skills training sessions were conducted in August and September by Emma and PDO, reaching a total of 39 participants, 27 females and 12 males including women, men, and young graduates from host community and IDPs. The trainings covered key personal and professional skills, such as self-awareness, confidence, emotional management, creativity, communication, teamwork, negotiation, problem-solving, and time and stress management. Through practical exercises, role-playing, and real-life examples, participants strengthened their life and employment skills, improved self-confidence, and enhanced their ability to cooperate and engage effectively with others. The sessions also promoted equality between men and women by ensuring equal access for women and supporting their professional development and economic independence. During the reporting period, PDO, Emma, and BWOCD delivered vocational trainings to strengthen women’s livelihoods and reduce risks linked to inequality between women and men. BWOCD held 2 trainings at the BWOCD Center in Mosul (sewing/tailoring and pastry/sweets) reaching 29 women and girls, Meanwhile , PDO delivered 3 sewing courses in Kabarto and Khanke camps reaching 23 women and girls (with 70% reporting improved skills), and Emma conducted 2 trainings in Qadya and Bersive 2 camps (salon skills and drawing) reaching 20women and girls. In total, 68 women and girls benefited, reporting increased confidence, motivation, and practical skills that can support income generation and greater household resilience. BWOCD also conducted a one-day employability skills workshop during the reporting period at the BWOCD Center in Mosul, targeting 13 young women (female graduates and students), the session focused on C.V. writing, interview skills, self-presentation, and confidence-building, and included a dedicated segment on workplace harassment awareness, prevention, and self-protection mechanisms.During the reported period, PDO conducted business and entrepreneurship training for 47 women in Khanke (town and camp) and Chamishku camp. The sessions covered basic business concepts and income generation. Participant feedback was positive, with increased motivation and interest in starting businesses, though some noted the need for additional financial support. As well Emma reporting period, Emma conducted two vocational training sessions in Sharya non-camp and Bersive 2 camps, reaching 23 women and one girl, focused on hand knitting. At the beginning, most participants had no prior experience with knitting or handcrafting, which created some challenges. However, through continuous practice and engagement, they showed clear improvement, became more confident, and experienced reduced overthinking and stress. By the end of the training, most participants had developed basic skills that could support small business initiatives. Similarly, BWOCD conducted one vocational training in sewing for 18 women and girls from low-income households with limited access to education and skills. The training covered both theoretical and practical aspects, including the use of sewing tools, basic tailoring, measurements, fabric cutting, and designing simple garments. Despite challenges such as limited experience and household responsibilities affecting attendance, flexible scheduling and continuous support helped ensure participation. As a result, participants gained practical skills, increased self-confidence, and improved their ability to pursue income-generating opportunities, while also benefiting from enhanced psychosocial well-being and a more positive outlook toward the future.

title.narrative: Number of business mentoring, networking and coaching sessions provided to women

description.narrative: During the first year of the programme, two networking sessions were organized by partners for 28 business owners, where new established business owners met with the already existing businesses and received advice from them but also increased coordination with each other in terms of work collaborations and/or client referrals. During the period from July till September 2025, three networking sessions were conducted for a total of 46 women entrepreneurs from Khanke town, Kabartu Camps, Bajid Kandala Camps, Chamishku Camp, Sharya town and Sharya, Qadiya, and Bersive Camps. The sessions provided a shared platform for peer learning and collaboration, enabled participants to exchange experiences, discuss challenges, and explore practical solutions for their businesses. Discussions focused on customer retention, marketing, product development, business expansion, and financial and administrative strategies, while emphasizing cooperation and peer support. The activity strengthened participants’ business skills, confidence, and visibility, fostered mutual motivation, and promoted the sustainability and growth of women-led micro-enterprises in both camp and non-camp areas. Moreover, 60 mentoring and coaching sessions were provided to a total of 60 women. During the period from January till March, Emma provided coaching and mentoring to women beneficiaries to support them before and during the establishment of their small businesses, following around 150 field interviews across target areas to assess needs and capacity, 25 women were selected and guided through practical steps such as project planning, basic financial management, pricing, and marketing, to strengthen sustainability, and the supported projects included tailoring, beauty/nail services, handicrafts, and small shops, helping women build confidence, increase income opportunities, and reduce economic pressure at household level.

title.narrative: Number of women attended business and management skills, desegregated by type of training.

description.narrative: The partners' livelihood officers, who received training from the Business Management consultant, created their own training materials with the consultant's support. They then conducted Business and Management skills training sessions for women and girls in the targeted locations. These women and girls were selected to receive small grants to start their own businesses. These training sessions not only improve the financial independence of women and girls but also boost their self-esteem, empowering them to stand up for their rights and avoid abusive situations. By entering the business world, these women challenge traditional gender roles, support gender equality, and promote their leadership in the community. Since the start of the programme, 248 women have been trained in business management, covering financial literacy, market understanding, marketing, and strategic planning. The trainings aimed to equip women to run small businesses successfully, fostering economic independence and resilience. During the period from July till September, PDO and Emma delivered business management training to reduce women’s economic dependency, one of the drivers of violence linked to inequality between women and men, by strengthening women’s ability to manage and sustain small businesses. PDO reached 25 women from Bajid Kandala, Chamishku, Kabarto, and Khanke camps, through individual/small-group coaching in the camps followed by a two-day course in Duhok covering marketing, market assessment, business identity, cost–benefit analysis, basic bookkeeping, and competitor analysis; post-tests showed learning gains, including improved skills in cost and profit tracking (64%) and entrepreneurship concepts (72%), meanwhile, smaller but important groups reported better knowledge of how to promote their products (32%) and differentiate themselves from competitors (16%). Emma also trained 25 women selected for livelihoods support through an intensive two-day course on entrepreneurship, pricing, customer service, simple marketing, financial management, and life skills (communication, time management, decision-making), which increased participants’ confidence and readiness to generate more stable income and sustain their projects. Overall, this brings the total to 390 women trained since the start of the programme in October 2023, covering financial literacy, market understanding, marketing, and strategic planning. The trainings aimed to equip women to run small businesses successfully, fostering economic independence and resilience.

title.narrative: OP 4.2: Established and strengthened micro-enterprises of conflict affected women.

description.narrative: The programme aims to empower women to establish and sustain small businesses that serve as a source of income and economic stability for them and their families. By establishing and strengthening small businesses, the programme seeks to enhance the economic empowerment and self-reliance of women in conflict-affected communities, ultimately fostering long-term socio-economic development and empowerment.

title.narrative: Number of new women supported with micro-enterprises

description.narrative: During April and May 2024, the Livelihood Officers of Emma, PDO and BWOCD started the process of gathering curriculum vitae and coordinated with Social Workers, diverse sectors, organisations, and Camp Management in targeted areas to identify qualified women who were interested in establishing their own businesses or growing their current ones. During the first year of the programme, the partners were able to support 66 women to start their own businesses based on the business ideas these women selected. During the reporting period, partners have identified women needing support to start their businesses and started the process by giving them trainings necessary, helping them develop their business plans and providing the financial support.During the reporting period, 16 women were supported with micro-enterprises through business management training and the provision of essential equipment and materials. The intervention enhanced women's financial independence, confidence, and self-reliance, while reducing vulnerability to economic violence and promoting sustainable income-generating activities. During July 2025 to September 2025, 38 women were supported with micro-enterprises through business management training and the provision of essential equipment and materials. The intervention enhanced women's financial independence, confidence, and self-reliance, while reducing vulnerability to economic violence and promoting sustainable income-generating activities. title.narrative: Number of previously supported women received additional support in terms of materials or grants, desegregated by type of support provided

description.narrative: During March 2024, the Livelihood Officers of the partners set plans to follow-up with the existing businesses and assess their needs. After an extensive assessment by the Livelihood Officers, ten already existing businesses received additional support. Before choosing these businesses a set of criteria were developed and interviews with women took place to see what their plans were in terms of improving or expanding their existing businesses. During the first year of the programme, partners were able to provide additional support to the 22 women who were supported before. These women were selected based on criteria developed by NPA and partners to ensure the sustainability and development of their businesses. One of the main criteria was that the business is contributing to elimination of violence based on inequality between women and men. During the reporting period, PDO and Emma continued strengthening women’s economic resilience in camp and non-camp areas of Duhok governorate by providing material support and mentoring to 44 women who already had small businesses. The intervention included in-kind tools, equipment, and guidance on business management, customer relations, and financial record-keeping. This support enhanced women’s financial independence, confidence, and visibility promoted the sustainability of their enterprises, and contributed to economic empowerment to reduce inequalities and vulnerability to violence.
