OP 3.5: Stakeholders have better understanding and promote equality between men and women concept and practices, violence based on inequality between women and men core concept and survivor-centred approaches.

description.narrative: The programme focuses on strengthening stakeholders’ knowledge and capacities related to equality concepts and practices, VAWG core principles, and survivor-centered approaches to service provision. Through targeted trainings and exchange forums, the programme aims to address misconceptions, improve attitudes and behaviours, and promote respectful engagement with VAWG survivors through enhancing awareness and practical understanding among governmental actors, community and religious leaders, CSOs, activists, media actors, university students, and community members, the programme contributes to creating a safer and more supportive environment for women, men, and survivors within the community.

title.narrative: Number of forums conducted to discuss the key areas towards women protection and empowerment, as well as survivor-centred approach service provision.

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the program, three forums were conducted in Sinjar under the Sinjar Dialogue Forum initiative by BWOCD. The forums brought together 85 participants (41 female and 44 male), including ISIS survivors, representatives from government institutions, and civil society actors. The discussions focused on the challenges faced by ISIS survivors in accessing services, justice, and decision-making, and included recommendations on coordination, institutional responsiveness, survivor participation, and follow-up mechanisms. The forums provided a safe and inclusive space for survivors to share experiences and increased their confidence in engaging with authorities and stakeholders. As part of the project’s efforts to strengthen women’s protection and empowerment through a survivor-centred approach, one exchange forum was organized by BWOCD on 22 December 2025 in Sinjar. The forum was conducted over one full day and brought together survivors, representatives of government institutions, and staff from civil society organizations who work directly with survivors. The forum created a safe and respectful space for women survivors to share their experiences and discuss barriers to accessing their rights, while engaging directly with duty bearers and service providers on the Yazidi Survivors Law (YSL), its implementation gaps, and the roles of government and NGOs in supporting survivors’ protection, dignity, and reintegration. Approximately 28 participants ( 13 Female, and 15 Male) attended, including survivors, government officials, and local/national NGOs, with survivors representing different age groups and backgrounds, some Key challenges were raised included loss of civil documentation and reports that some judges require survivor witnesses a condition not stated in the Yazidi Survivors Law which was highlighted as a major barrier to justice.

title.narrative: Number of people (governmental entities, community/religious leaders, community members, CSOs, activists, media actors, and university students, etc.) capacitated on equality between men and women concept and practices, Violence based on inequality between women and men core concept and survivor-centred approach service provision.

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the programme 99 individuals from various stakeholders in Duhok were capacitated on equality between men and women concept and best practices. The training sessions aimed to enhance understanding and promote the concept of gender equality and its practices, as well as eliminating misconceptions of feminism was discussed by Emma with their training participants. It focused on increasing awareness of gender equality concepts, SVAWG core principles, and respectful engagement with SVAWG survivors seeking services from stakeholders. By enhancing the capacity, knowledge, and awareness of the participants, the training sought to foster a more equitable environment. All participants had more than three years working experience, however a considerable number of them expressed that this is the first time they have participated in a training like this, especially those who were working in the education or journalism sector. While NGOs and other actors were very active over the last 10 years in providing essential capacity building to the stakeholders, it was noticed that these efforts have been reduced due to decrease in the number of NGOs in Duhok governorate. A concern previously raised by NPA partners, that there are many new faces working with actors that are involved directly or indirectly in SVAWG prevention and response. These new individuals need more comprehensive training sessions especially on how to work with survivors in a sensitive and respectful manner. During the second year, two major stakeholder trainings were conducted to strengthen awareness of equality between men and women, legal protections framework, and social issues among diverse community actors and institutions. In September 2025, a two-day workshop was conducted by Emma, bringing together 19 participants 15 females and 4 males from diverse backgrounds. The participants included both genders, different age groups, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and members of the host community. They represented various professions such as psychology, sociology, nursing, social work, and teaching, and belonged to different religious groups, including Muslims, Christians, and Yezidis. The workshop covered topics such as United Nation Security Council Resolution (UNSCR) 1325, local laws, feminism, and protection frameworks, which were new to many participants. The diverse group shared personal experiences, discussed gaps in legal awareness, and expressed strong interest in further workshops. The second was a three-day training on Equality and Equality Mainstreaming, conducted by PDO from 24 to 26 August 2025 in Duhok, attended by 13 participants including 6 females and 7 males representatives of universities, NGOs, government institutions, and community actors. The training focused on inclusivity concepts, VAWG dynamics, survivor-centered approaches, power relations, and the link between MHPSS and equality. Participants engaged in practical exercises and discussions, emphasizing the need for stronger gender-sensitive policies and inclusive practices. The trainings enhanced participants’ overall understanding of equality, legal protection frameworks, and VAWG dynamics, while strengthening their ability to apply responsive and survivor-centered approaches within their professional and community roles contributing to a more informed, and responsive engagement. On International volunteer day, Emma conducted a capacity building workshops for a group of six 6 volunteers (4 Female, and 2 Male) focusing on inequality between women and men and mainstreaming equality between women and men. The workshops aimed to deepen participants’ understanding of key concepts, principles, and practical approaches, including prevention, safe referral pathways, and survivor-centred engagement. These sessions also served as a sustainability measure, as the trained volunteers are expected to remain active within their communities, support individuals in need, raise awareness, and act as key links to available services even after the program comes to an end.

title.narrative: OP 3.1: Quality case management and referral services provided for women and girls 15+ who are at risk or survivors of Violence based on inequality between women and men .

description.narrative: This output is dedicated to strengthening the support services for women and girls 15+, who have experienced the impact of conflict accompanied by the violence based on inequality between men and women. The aim is to provide a tailored and holistic approach towards the recovery and reintegration of these women and girls. The programme focuses on delivering tailored case management services, ensuring that each survivor receives support that is aligned with her unique needs. This approach aims to empower women and girls to regain agency and control over their lives. Additionally, the programme emphasizes the importance of referrals to specialised services, ranging from medical and legal support to MHPSS and governmental support. By facilitating connectionto these vital services, the programme seeks to address the multifaceted needs of survivors and contribute to their holistic recovery. Continuous support is at the core of this programme, as reflected in the follow-up calls provided to survivors who receive referrals. Lastly, the programme recognizes the significance of meeting immediate and urgent needs, offering simple services such as in-kind support and non-food items as well as other needs that might arise and need to be dressed urgently. This approach contributes to theoverall well-being of survivors and contributes to their empowerment and resilience.

title.narrative: Percentage of cases receiving referrals that have received a follow up call within one week after referral.

description.narrative: During the reporting period, 394 cases were refereed to different service providers. While survivors require various case management services, the program efficiently addresses many of these needs. However, there are instances where survivors may need specialized services. In such cases, social workers play a crucial role by referring survivors to the available specialized services. The referral process is particularly important given the reduction of services in multiple locations, especially the camps in KRI. NPA and partners actively coordinate with existing service providers and other stakeholders to comprehensively map out available services and stay updated on the latest available services.

title.narrative: Number of women and girls 15+ received case management services.

title.narrative: Number of women and girls receiving simple needs (in-kind, NFI, etc.) services

Apart from the need for MHPSS, medical and legal services, the need for immediate food or NFI is still apparent. Since the beggining of the programme 652 survivors benefited from simple needs, of which most received food items, other categories included; medicines, hygiene kits and clothes.

title.narrative: Number of counselling sessions and follow-ups provided to women and girls +15 (open cases).

After the action plan, the social workers follow up on each survivor till all their needs are met or till the survivors are at a point where they no longer need any more counselling sessions. Since the beginning of the program 4139.

title.narrative: OP1.2: CSO partners have better organizational capacity (e.g., project management, Human Resources, MEAL, Logistics and Procurement, Security and Financial Management capacities).

In total 12 participants benefited from this training. The training focused on the Fundamentals of Using Cash and Accrual Basis, Preparation of Financial Statements and Managing Currency Differences and preparing the budget and trail balance. The training lasted for three days and was held in Duhok. The overall knowledge increase was 14.73% and the feedback of the participants was very positive. NPA conducted a refresher anti-corruption training was provided to two of the protection partners during the last quarter PDO and Emma, the training aimed to strengthen ethical practices and internal compliance systems while deepening participants’ understanding of integrity principal. In total 26 participants (19 female and 5 male) benefited from the training, and focused on raising awareness of corruption risks, promoting transparency, and reinforcing accountability. This contributed to improved data management and reporting accuracy.

title.narrative: Number of CSO partners that have demonstrated improved security management capacity, ranking ‘satisfactory’ in NPA capacity assessment.

description.narrative: Continuing the efforts that NPA with Sida support initiated in February 2023, NPA conducted a three-day Security and Safety Training for all NPA partners in December 2024 (including those under this grant, one security focal point per organization). In total 13 participants (two women and 11 men) and two NPA staff (both male) participated in this training. The aim of this training was to provide NPA’s partners with the necessary skills to identify and analyse security risks in their respective areas of operation, enabling them to effectively handle emergency situations and maintain the safety and security of their staff. The Security and Safety Training was theoretical and practical, and included topics such as: Security principles, security strategies, context analysis, risk analysis, crisis management, and first aid. The overall knowledge increase was 119% and the feedback of the participants was very positive. In March 2026, NPA security team provided a two-day training on Risk Analysis and Crisis Management. Due to the ongoing security concerns caused by the new conflict between Iran and United States of America, that had direct effects on the northern Iraq, this training was deemed necessary. Apart from this training, many security sessions were provided to partners.

title.narrative: Strengthened Civil Society Organisations function more independently and effectively in implementing stability and protection interventions in Iraq.

Number of CSO partners who receive an overall ‘high’ score on NPA’s Organisational Development Dialogue Assessment Tool (ODDAT) [The tool measures the score under five assessment areas: 1. The policy of the organisation; 2. The internal democracy and unity of the organisation; 3. Capacity to influence, have impact and make changes; 4. Capacity to relate to, and make alliances with, other actors; and 5. The technical and administrative competences of the organisation]

description.narrative: In December 2023, NPA conducted the ODDAT for the partners. While all partners showed satisfactory performance across the five key assessment areas, improvement was seen as necessary. Partners showed readiness to enhance their policies, especially in areas where organizational policies might accurately reflect strategic objectives. title.narrative: OP 1.4: CSO partners’ Women Community Centres and satellite safe spaces are functional for confidential counselling and indoor recreation and continue operating in the selected areas.
Number of mobile spaces that are equipped by partners to conduct activities in the camps and non-camp areas.

description.narrative: Emma, PDO and BWO have three static centres open and functioning. Apart from that Emma and PDO have six mobile spaces, one is a rented centre in Sharya town and five are spaces received from camp management to conduct activities in the camps of Kabarto, Qadia, Chammishko, Bajid Kandala, and Bersive. There used to be two Bersive camps, however the two camps are now merged in one, which means that in order to cover the big camp apart from receiving the space, Emma needs to conduct door to door activities as part of outreach; as well as for those families that are far from the centre. This is the same approach that PDO adopted to cover Kabarto 1, Kabarto 2 and Chammishko camp, which is one of the biggest IDPs camps in Iraq. Given that the services are reducing in camps while some other camps have no case management services at all, partners often find themselves overwhelmed with cases referred to them. Apart from that many NGOs have reported during meetings that the domestic violence has increased as a result of the camp closure news, because many families had disagreements among themselves leading to physical violence sometimes. During November 2024, BWOCD opened a mobile space in Sinjar to facilitate the implementation of activities for the ISIS survivors in Sinjar.

description.narrative: The survivors are usually met during or at the closure stage of case management to see their satisfaction and whether there are areas that partners can develop. All interviews are done with utmost confidentiality and with informed consent of the survivor. During the first year of the programme, the satisfaction was 100% by survivors (44% ranked their satisfaction 4 and 56% ranked their satisfaction 5), they attributed this satisfaction to the good listening skills of the social workers, the care and empathy they received as well as the constant follow up and referral. NPA and partners will ensure this positive feedback from survivors will continue and that the needs of survivors will always be met with care and respect. The satisfaction of the survivors till the time of the reporting is 97%, most survivors attribute this to the respect shown to them, their needs that were met and how their conditions improved exponentiality after receiving the case management. However, one trend that partners noticed due to the US-funding freeze is the fact that in most camps the partners are now the only service providers, which adds to the pressure of reduced services.
